messages.subject: Re: warnings in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Lucia-

It is simply letting you know that it has restricted the power parameter
of the hazard rate at the lower bound set in the program.  This occurs
when the data are such that the number of observations declines quickly
with distance.  It may suggest the need to truncate some data in the
tail or a problem with distance measurement or it may simply be
representing a situation in which detection is declining rapidly.  Only
you can determine that with your data.  It does mean that it is likely
that the best hazard rate function would even have a lower power.  Look
in the documentation.  I believe you can set the lower bound that it uses.

regards --jeff

messages.subject: Re: warnings in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
What value did you use for the bound?  You can't let it get to 0. Even
anything really small will create an unrealistic detection function that
is difficult to integrate.  Start off by making the bound slightly
smaller than the current bound until it misbehaves or converges to
something other than the lower bound.  Send me a picture of the plot
off-list and some more details about the data collection and how many
observations you have.

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: warnings in MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Lucia, (cc list),

It sounds to me like you have very spiked data (ie a very large=20
proportion of your observations are at, or close to zero distance).=20
This can be a big problem for distance sampling analyses.  As Jeff said=20
before, you need to understand why it happened, and do something about=20
it if possible.  Truncation may be an option.  Below, I have pasted some=20
text from a manuscript about a salvage method for coping with spiked=20
line transect data caused by cutting straight lines through dense=20
tropical vegetation.  The manuscript has now been revised, and is still=20
in review, but I thought the text might be useful to you in considering=20
why the spike may have occurred and what to do about it.  The text=20
contains plenty of references to the Buckland et al. (2001) book=20
Introduction to Distance Sampling, which has longer explanations of many=20
of these issues.

Hope this helps - if you'd like to discuss this more I suggest we take=20
it up off the list.

Cheers,

  - Len

Abstract from an older version of the in review manuscript "Estimating=20
forest ungulate density from "spiked" line transect data." by=20
Gangadharan, A., N.S. Kumar, L. Thomas and K.U. Karanth.

Causes of spiked data and possible solutions
A spike at zero distance may occur due to several reasons. In general,=20
there are five potential causes of spiked distance data: (1) observers=20
concentrating survey effort on or very close to the transect line; (2)=20
heterogeneity in detection probability caused by factors in addition to=20
distance from line; (3) observers rounding perpendicular distances or=20
sighting angles of animals detected close to the line to zero; (4)=20
animals being attracted to the observers or to the transect line; (5)=20
enhanced visibility along the transect line relative to just off the=20
line. All of these may occur in forest surveys, but last two are most=20
clearly associated with transect lines cut through vegetation.  We=20
briefly review each cause below.

Although field procedures should ensure that all animals at zero=20
distance are detected, concentrating survey effort on the immediate=20
vicinity of the transect line to the exclusion of effort at moderate=20
distances (=93guarding the centreline=94, Buckland et al., 2001: 30-31;=20
Burnham et al., 2004: 345-46) leads to a steep decline in the detection=20
function at small perpendicular distances, and a distribution of=20
observed distances with a spike close to zero that is hard to fit=20
accurately. Using the standard key function and series expansion=20
formulation of Buckland et al. (2001: 58-61) to fit detection functions=20
to the distance data, and Akaike=92s Information Criterion (AIC) to selec=
t=20
the most parsimonious model, the selected model will usually be one that=20
under-fits the spike, given small to moderate sample sizes. This will=20
result in an overestimate of average detection probability and hence an=20
underestimate of density. With larger sample sizes, the selected model=20
may fit the spike, but often has high variance. At the analysis stage,=20
it may be difficult to distinguish the results of =93guarding the=20
centreline=94 from that of animal attraction to the observer or line,=20
without additional knowledge of the animals=92 biology and field methods=20
used. However, if this is known to be the sole cause of the spike, only=20
models that fit the observed spike well (rather than those with lowest=20
AIC) should be considered during analysis.

Perpendicular distance from the transect line is not the only factor=20
influencing the probability of detecting an animal cluster. However,=20
ignoring these other factors and modelling detection of just=20
perpendicular distance usually leads to little or no bias in density=20
estimates, due to the =93pooling robustness=94 property of the standard=20
detection function estimators (Buckland et al., 2001: 41-42; Burnham et=20
al., 2004: 389-392). However, if these factors have a very strong=20
effect, they can lead to a spiked detection function, and a resulting=20
tendency to underestimate density (see previous paragraph). A study area=20
may be a mixture of open habitats, where animals can easily be seen at=20
large distances, and closed habitats, where detection is only possible=20
at small distances. For a species that occurs in both habitats,=20
modelling detections from both habitats together results in a composite=20
detection function with a spike in detection probability at small=20
perpendicular distances. However, heterogeneity must be extreme to=20
generate a large spike (Thomas et al. unpublished data). One solution if=20
the causes of the heterogeneity can be measured is to include them as=20
covariates in an MCDS analysis (Marques et al., in press). However, this=20
may bias results if the spike in closed habitats is exacerbated by=20
reasons other than habitat heterogeneity (see below); the selected model=20
may then overfit the spike in closed habitats and hence overestimate=20
density.

Observer rounding of small perpendicular distances or angles to zero is=20
a form of measurement error that can produce a substantial spike in=20
observations. If sighting distance and angle data are collected,=20
rounding can often be prevented by using measurement aids such as=20
rangefinders for distances and compasses for angles. Rounding to zero=20
angle can also occur if it is not clear exactly where the transect line=20
is, and this can be solved by clearly marking the line. If rounding is=20
known to have occurred, perhaps the best analytic solution is to avoid=20
using functions that fit the spike (Buckland et al. 2001: 263-68).

A transect cut through dense vegetation may either becomes used as a=20
trail by animals or create preferred edge habitat (Buckland et al. 2001:=20
293-94), resulting in higher density of animals on the transect line=20
than elsewhere in the surveyed strip. As noted earlier, this problem can=20
be difficult to distinguish from observers concentrating survey effort=20
on the line; a potential solution is to use auxiliary information on=20
animal density perpendicular to the line (for example through strip=20
transects for dung) to jointly estimate animal density and detection=20
function on the main transects. Animal use of transects as trails may be=20
unavoidable in areas with impenetrable undergrowth, where cutting of=20
lines is essential for passage of observers but also simultaneously=20
opens up areas for passage of animals.

The final cause of spiked line transect data is enhanced visibility=20
along the transect line relative to just off it, caused when transects=20
are cut through thick vegetation. This will artificially increase the=20
number of observations on and near the line but not at larger=20
perpendicular distances (Buckland et al. 2001: 294-95), and hence the=20
number of detections will fall off sharply with distance from the line.=20
This problem may be exacerbated when the cut transects are straight;=20
observers can then see far ahead of them along the line and will count=20
animals that are crossing the transect line far in front of them,=20
further inflating counts on the line. Thus, even moderate levels of=20
animal movement will lead to a relatively large number of detections at=20
zero distance. This represents a violation of the standard assumption=20
that animals are detected at their initial location, or equivalently=20
that the survey occurs at an =93instant=94 in time (Buckland et al. 2001:=
=20
31). In this circumstance, na=EFve application of the standard analysis=20
methods may underestimate average detection probability, because the=20
detection function model with the lowest AIC may be one that fits the=20
spike, and hence overestimate density. One analytic solution is to use=20
only detection function models that do not fit the spike, such as the=20
half-normal key function with no adjustment terms. When using MCDS=20
methods to select among potential other covariates, however, model=20
selection may be influenced by those covariates that lead to models that=20
best fit the spike.

We propose an alternative analytic solution, =93forward truncation=94, ba=
sed=20
on Gangadharan (2005), where observations made beyond some subjectively=20
chosen distance in front of the observer are removed before analysis,=20
thereby reducing the effect of animal movement on the data and=20
potentially increasing the reliability of MCDS analyses. This =93forward=20
truncation=94 distance should be chosen so that as many as possible of th=
e=20
observations at zero perpendicular distances are removed, while=20
minimally affecting the frequencies of larger distances.

A better solution to the problems caused by cutting transect lines is to=20
revise field methods so that vegetation is minimally cleared. Where the=20
line passes through patches of thick vegetation, it is acceptable to=20
walk around them provided the deviation is not so far that animals on=20
the line could be missed, and perpendicular distances are taken relative=20
to the nominal transect line rather than the actual path walked. It is=20
therefore essential to mark the line prominently so that observers know=20
exactly where it is at all times. Detailed recommendations of field=20
methods for forest surveys are provided by Karanth et al. (2002).

enhanced visibility along the transect line relative to just off the=20
line. All of these may occur in forest surveys, but last two are most=20
clearly associated with transect lines cut through vegetation.  We=20
briefly review each cause below.

Although field procedures should ensure that all animals at zero=20
distance are detected, concentrating survey effort on the immediate=20
vicinity of the transect line to the exclusion of effort at moderate=20
distances (=93guarding the centreline=94, Buckland et al., 2001: 30-31;=20
Burnham et al., 2004: 345-46) leads to a steep decline in the detection=20
function at small perpendicular distances, and a distribution of=20
observed distances with a spike close to zero that is hard to fit=20
accurately. Using the standard key function and series expansion=20
formulation of Buckland et al. (2001: 58-61) to fit detection functions=20
to the distance data, and Akaike=92s Information Criterion (AIC) to selec=
t=20
the most parsimonious model, the selected model will usually be one that=20
under-fits the spike, given small to moderate sample sizes. This will=20
result in an overestimate of average detection probability and hence an=20
underestimate of density. With larger sample sizes, the selected model=20
may fit the spike, but often has high variance. At the analysis stage,=20
it may be difficult to distinguish the results of =93guarding the=20
centreline=94 from that of animal attraction to the observer or line,=20
without additional knowledge of the animals=92 biology and field methods=20
used. However, if this is known to be the sole cause of the spike, only=20
models that fit the observed spike well (rather than those with lowest=20
AIC) should be considered during analysis.

Perpendicular distance from the transect line is not the only factor=20
influencing the probability of detecting an animal cluster. However,=20
ignoring these other factors and modelling detection of just=20
perpendicular distance usually leads to little or no bias in density=20
estimates, due to the =93pooling robustness=94 property of the standard=20
detection function estimators (Buckland et al., 2001: 41-42; Burnham et=20
al., 2004: 389-392). However, if these factors have a very strong=20
effect, they can lead to a spiked detection function, and a resulting=20
tendency to underestimate density (see previous paragraph). A study area=20
may be a mixture of open habitats, where animals can easily be seen at=20
large distances, and closed habitats, where detection is only possible=20
at small distances. For a species that occurs in both habitats,=20
modelling detections from both habitats together results in a composite=20
detection function with a spike in detection probability at small=20
perpendicular distances. However, heterogeneity must be extreme to=20
generate a large spike (Thomas et al. unpublished data). One solution if=20
the causes of the heterogeneity can be measured is to include them as=20
covariates in an MCDS analysis (Marques et al., in press). However, this=20
may bias results if the spike in closed habitats is exacerbated by=20
reasons other than habitat heterogeneity (see below); the selected model=20
may then overfit the spike in closed habitats and hence overestimate=20
density.

Observer rounding of small perpendicular distances or angles to zero is=20
a form of measurement error that can produce a substantial spike in=20
observations. If sighting distance and angle data are collected,=20
rounding can often be prevented by using measurement aids such as=20
rangefinders for distances and compasses for angles. Rounding to zero=20
angle can also occur if it is not clear exactly where the transect line=20
is, and this can be solved by clearly marking the line. If rounding is=20
known to have occurred, perhaps the best analytic solution is to avoid=20
using functions that fit the spike (Buckland et al. 2001: 263-68).

A transect cut through dense vegetation may either becomes used as a=20
trail by animals or create preferred edge habitat (Buckland et al. 2001:=20
293-94), resulting in higher density of animals on the transect line=20
than elsewhere in the surveyed strip. As noted earlier, this problem can=20
be difficult to distinguish from observers concentrating survey effort=20
on the line; a potential solution is to use auxiliary information on=20
animal density perpendicular to the line (for example through strip=20
transects for dung) to jointly estimate animal density and detection=20
function on the main transects. Animal use of transects as trails may be=20
unavoidable in areas with impenetrable undergrowth, where cutting of=20
lines is essential for passage of observers but also simultaneously=20
opens up areas for passage of animals.

The final cause of spiked line transect data is enhanced visibility=20
along the transect line relative to just off it, caused when transects=20
are cut through thick vegetation. This will artificially increase the=20
number of observations on and near the line but not at larger=20
perpendicular distances (Buckland et al. 2001: 294-95), and hence the=20
number of detections will fall off sharply with distance from the line.=20
This problem may be exacerbated when the cut transects are straight;=20
observers can then see far ahead of them along the line and will count=20
animals that are crossing the transect line far in front of them,=20
further inflating counts on the line. Thus, even moderate levels of=20
animal movement will lead to a relatively large number of detections at=20
zero distance. This represents a violation of the standard assumption=20
that animals are detected at their initial location, or equivalently=20
that the survey occurs at an =93instant=94 in time (Buckland et al. 2001:=
=20
31). In this circumstance, na=EFve application of the standard analysis=20
methods may underestimate average detection probability, because the=20
detection function model with the lowest AIC may be one that fits the=20
spike, and hence overestimate density. One analytic solution is to use=20
only detection function models that do not fit the spike, such as the=20
half-normal key function with no adjustment terms. When using MCDS=20
methods to select among potential other covariates, however, model=20
selection may be influenced by those covariates that lead to models that=20
best fit the spike.

We propose an alternative analytic solution, =93forward truncation=94, ba=
sed=20
on Gangadharan (2005), where observations made beyond some subjectively=20
chosen distance in front of the observer are removed before analysis,=20
thereby reducing the effect of animal movement on the data and=20
potentially increasing the reliability of MCDS analyses. This =93forward=20
truncation=94 distance should be chosen so that as many as possible of th=
e=20
observations at zero perpendicular distances are removed, while=20
minimally affecting the frequencies of larger distances.

A better solution to the problems caused by cutting transect lines is to=20
revise field methods so that vegetation is minimally cleared. Where the=20
line passes through patches of thick vegetation, it is acceptable to=20
walk around them provided the deviation is not so far that animals on=20
the line could be missed, and perpendicular distances are taken relative=20
to the nominal transect line rather than the actual path walked. It is=20
therefore essential to mark the line prominently so that observers know=20
exactly where it is at all times. Detailed recommendations of field=20
methods for forest surveys are provided by Karanth et al. (2002).

messages.subject: sampling question
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
I am sampling urban birds in residential areas. Line transects are limited =
to public streets. The habitat is stratified in narrow bands. Typically, a =
four-lane street has two traffic lanes in the center and a parking lane at =
each curbside. Next is a narrow pedestrian lane on either side. In some cou=
ntries residential lots are enclosed by high walls along their perimeter, w=
hich restrict visual detection. In the USA custom and regulations tend to p=
rohibit such walls so that there is a band of front yards, usually with gra=
ss lawns and good visibility, then a row of houses, and finally a row of re=
ar yards, typically enclosed with high privacy fences.=A0Birds perching on =
the proximal side of roofs can be detected but those on the distal side can=
not. Birds in the rear yards are frequently heard but seldom seen.
=A0
In older neighborhoods a line of utility poles is usually situated between =
the street and pedestrian walk along one side of the street. These poles ha=
ve multiple layers of wires; a ground wire at the top, 2 or more electric l=
ines below that, and various telephone and TV cable lines lower down. These=
 multiple wires provide favorite perches for birds. Trees may be present al=
ong one or both sides of the street, but heavily pruned adjacent to the wir=
es. Birds perched on the wires are numerous and conspicuous and detection i=
s close to 1. Birds in tree canopies have detection less than one.
=A0
While traversing the street centerline would preserve habitat symmetry, saf=
ety reasons preclude this. The observer can choose to walk beneath the util=
ity lines and produce heaping in the 0 to 3 meter range, or walk on the opp=
osite side of the street and produce heaping in the 8 to 12 meter range. Ar=
e there any theoretical reasons why an observer should choose one side of t=
he street or the other?
=A0
Robert W. McFarlane
Houston, Texas, USA

Below, I reproduce a page from Chapter 1 of the Users guide that answers
your general question about recommended literature.  Your specific
questions about the different detection functions are answered in
chapters 1-3 of the introductory book.  The book is written with
different users in mind, but chapters 1 and 2 are hopefully quite
accessable to biologists, as are the later chapters on line and point
transects, with their worked examples.  Perhaps others can suggest
introductory (but necessarily less comprehensive) texts.

Good luck with your work,

  - Len Thomas

------------------------------------------------------------------------
Distance Sampling Reference Books

The standard reference for conventional distance sampling methods is:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. 2001. Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

The book describes the methods in detail, as well as covering aspects of
survey design and giving several worked examples.  It updates the
previous standard work:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P. and Laake, J.L. 1993.
Distance Sampling: Estimating Abundance of Biological Populations.
Chapman and Hall, London, reprinted 1999 by RUWPA, University of St.
Andrews, Scotland.

The 1993 book is still available for download over the internet at no
charge, at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/

The advanced methods in this software are described in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. (editors) 2004. Advanced Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

This book describes automated survey design methods, multiple covariate
distance sampling and mark-recapture distance sampling.  In addition
methods are described that are not currently in Distance but which we
hope to include in the future, such as spatial modelling of density and
adaptive distance sampling.

messages.subject: Re: model definitions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Martin,

Below, I reproduce a page from Chapter 1 of the Users guide that answers
your general question about recommended literature.  Your specific
questions about the different detection functions are answered in
chapters 1-3 of the introductory book.  The book is written with
different users in mind, but chapters 1 and 2 are hopefully quite
accessable to biologists, as are the later chapters on line and point
transects, with their worked examples.  Perhaps others can suggest
introductory (but necessarily less comprehensive) texts.

Good luck with your work,

  - Len Thomas

------------------------------------------------------------------------
Distance Sampling Reference Books

The standard reference for conventional distance sampling methods is:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. 2001. Introduction to Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

The book describes the methods in detail, as well as covering aspects of
survey design and giving several worked examples.  It updates the
previous standard work:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P. and Laake, J.L. 1993.
Distance Sampling: Estimating Abundance of Biological Populations.
Chapman and Hall, London, reprinted 1999 by RUWPA, University of St.
Andrews, Scotland.

The 1993 book is still available for download over the internet at no
charge, at:

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.book/

The advanced methods in this software are described in the following book:

Buckland, S.T., Anderson, D.R., Burnham, K.P., Laake, J.L., Borchers,
D.L. and Thomas, L. (editors) 2004. Advanced Distance Sampling. Oxford
University Press, London.

This book describes automated survey design methods, multiple covariate
distance sampling and mark-recapture distance sampling.  In addition
methods are described that are not currently in Distance but which we
hope to include in the future, such as spatial modelling of density and
adaptive distance sampling.

messages.subject: Re: sampling question
messages.body_plain:
Robert,

When one does not walk randomly located transect lines, then a critical
assumption of standard distance sampling is violated: that the true
distribution of animals with respect to distance is known.  Therefore
any change in frequency of detections with distance for a line transect
cannot be interpreted as indicating change in detectability - it could
be that or it could be change in density.  In other words, standard
distance sampling methods do not apply.  Tiago Marques devoted much of
his PhD thesis to an examination of these issues, and (somewhat complex)
methods for trying to get around them - I recommend you have a look at
it.  A copy is at http://hdl.handle.net/10023/391  See also the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book section 7.8.5.

It seems to me that you could consider
(a) a strip transect of out to a distance where every animal of the
target species is detectable.  This will only give you density in this
strip however, and not density in the town.
(b) a separate study to get at detectability (for example where you have
people visually tracking animals to set up "trials" for the line
transect observer and then doing logistic regression to get the
detection function), so that you can then estimate the density gradient.
  There may be something about this in Tiago's thesis.

As for your specific question about where to walk: I think you have far
bigger concerns to address, as outlined above!

All the best,

  - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: estimating N for strata not used to fit model
messages.subject_clean: estimating N for strata not used to fit model
messages.body_plain:
Frank, (list),

If you want to estimate density by some strata then you don't
necessarily need to use MCDS to fit a factor for each observer, or site
and year (if they are not the strata you wish to estimate density for).
  The pooling robustness property of conventional distance sampling
estimators means that you will incur little bias if you have estimates
of detection function at the level at which you want to estimate
density, and it doesn't matter (within limits) if there are factors
within that that affect detectability but which you don't model.  This
is covered in various places in the literature; my favourite at present
is Marques et al. (2007) The Auk 124:1229--1243. (but as a coauthor, I'm
biased!).  A copy of this paper is at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/len/papers/MarquesAuk2007.pdf
So, a good bet might be to try MCDS with the strata you are actually
interested in as covariates.

But you don't have to do it this way - if model selection statistics
(and common sense) tells you that site and year are better covariates by
all means use them.  You can still set up a distance project with the
stratum level being the strata you want to estimate density for, and
site and year at some lower level (substrata, or sample, or whatever).
If you send me some more specific information about exactly what you
want to do (off the list), I can suggest a way to set up a project to do
it.  The key then is that you want to fit the model to the covariates,
but estimate detectability by stratum -- in the MCDS engine, Estimate
tab, under Detection function, you tick both the global and stratum
boxes.  This is covered in the MCDS chapter of the Users Guide in the
topic "Estimating the Detection Function at Multiple Levels" -- although
it's obviously not easy to find or not clear as people often ask how to
do this.

Hope this helps,

  - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: Patchy distributions
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jennifer,

I didn't see any replies to your question on the list, so I'll have a
stab at it.  If anyone else did reply to you off the list, can you
please collate or summarize the responses into 1 email and post them, so
they are in the archive for others to see.

If you can predict in advance where the high rockfish concentrations are
likely to be, you could consider stratifying the survey into high
density and low density areas.  The high density stratum does not have
to be one continuous polygon.  You could use the same survey methods in
this stratum, or something different.  But if the food location is not
predictable then this will not work.

Again, if it were not an ephemeral resource the fish were cueing on, you
could consider spatial density surface modelling (Chapter 4 of the
Advanced Distance Sampling book) rather than the conventional
design-based methods for encounter rate -- but if you don't have the
right covariates available with will not work either.

If the feeding aggregations are easy to spot using a "fast" survey
method that can quickly cover a large part of your study area, you could
consider using that method for the feeding aggregations, and sticking to
the regular line transect method for the non-feeding fish, and then
summing the two abundance estimates from the different surveys to get
the total abundance.  If you encounter a feeding aggregation on the
regular line transect survey you would ignore it, as it is part of the
"fast" survey.  But this may not work in your case if it's not easy to
unambiguously define what constitutes a feeding aggregation, or if a
"fast" survey is not possible.

Perhaps others have further suggestion?

Cheers,

  - Len

--

messages.subject: Re: shifting observation to reduce observer bias
messages.subject_clean: shifting observation to reduce observer bias
messages.body_plain:
Ai,

I didn't see a reply on the list, so I'll have a stab at it.

Ask yourself how far the bird could have been attracted from.  If you
can answer this question, you could consider turning your data from
"exact" distance measurements into intervals (this is done in the data
filter), where the first interval includes the farthest distance from
which a bird could have been attracted.  The other (farther out)
interval widths are not important - you could perhaps have 5-6 intervals
in total (see introductory book section 5.5).  This way, all the animals
that "should" be in the first interval are there, so your movement
problem goes away.  Seems to me preferable to the approach you
described.  This won't work well if the first interval is wider than the
"shoulder" in the detection function -- ie the first cutpoint is at a
location where probability of detection is significantly less than 1.

There's lots of great advice on field and analysis methods for point
transect studies of songbirds in Buckland (2006) "Point transect surveys
for songbirds: robust methodologies", The Auk 123:345-345.  A copy of
the text from paper is online at
http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/stb/songbird.pdf

Hope this helps,

  - Len

messages.body_plain:
Jennifer, Len, and List,

Just thought I would provide one more thought to your problem.  Conroy
et al. have a paper in press in Ecology entitled, Efficient estimation
of abundance for patchily distributed populations via two-phase,
adaptive sampling.  I am not sure when it will be out, but I have seen
the proof so it should be coming out soon.  Essentially, the paper
describes a way to estimate occupancy on all selected or random sites
(phase 1); the second phase kicks in when some threshold of detection
occurs and then a more intensive method of sampling (e.g. CMR and
distance sampling) can be used to estimate abundance.  So for your
situation as I understand it, you could use phase 1 to "map" the areas
thet are normally distributed and use distance sampling for schools.
Through a joint likelihood you get detection probabilities and abundance.

Just a thought.

James

give very different density estimates.

evasive movement!  If for example you have too few detections in your
first interval and too many in your second interval because of this

falls off steeply from the 2nd to the 3rd interval.  If this is what is
happening, you should not left-truncate.  Distance will then tend to
average out the lack of animals in the 1st interval with the surplus of
animals in the 2nd interval, and you should then get less biased density
estimates.  Of course, the goodness-of-fit test is likely to indicate
that you have a poor fit - but that is due to a problem with the data
more than a problem with the model.

Yes, in fact, the detection function in MRDS performs slightly worse =

the
output file there are several histogram tables of probabilities of
detection. One is the global, and then there are separate ones for each
level of the covariate used (only one covariate used in this model). For
some reason the histograms are divided into 140 bins (not sure if this =
is by
default or one can modify this somewhere). If I get the average =
probability
of detection for the global table, I get 0.3063, very close to the =
average p
provided by Distance for this model in the summary of results (0.3072). =
In
the same way, I can get the average p for the three levels of the =
covariate,
which, theoretically, would be the p for the sightings that have that =
level
of covariate. So all the sightings done in sea state 0 would have a
probability of detection of 0.48,71, with sea state 1 it would be =
0.3195,
and with sea state 2 0.0514, which makes sense. So theoretically the =
problem
would be easily solved.=20

But I would like to get confirmation from Len that this is the way to do =
it,
because I am not 100% sure given the small difference between the =
average p
provided by the Distance results summary, and the average I calculate =
from
the histograms. Maybe I am missing something?

Cheers,
Ana

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I was searching through the archives for an answer to a particular
question, and found that it had been asked before but may not have
received an answer at the time. I'm quoting the mail below.

Basically, the question is: can a parameter that has been used in a MCDS
model as a covariate of detection probability later also be used as a
predictor of density in, say, a regression analysis of the resulting
density estimates? Or does this confound the effects of the covariate on
detection probability and density?

If this has been covered before, please point me in the right direction!

cheers
florian

quote:
-----------------

Jeff and others:

Please correct me if I am wrong.  I am sending the following comments and
question because I am new to distance sampling and want to learn more.

I think the best estimates of density will be those from the best model
for detection probability.  However, I do not think the model for
detection probability tells you anything about how the covariates
influence true density.  It only tells you how the covariates influence
detection probability and thereby influence the count data.  You will need
to use linear regression or some other analysis to model your density
estimates as a function of your landscape/habitat variables.

What I do not know and would like to know is - if you find grass had a
negative influence on density after finding that grass also had a negative
influence on detection probability, can you draw any conclusions about the
relationship between grass and density?  That is, will the effects of
grass on density be confounded with effects of grass on detection
probability, or will incorporation of detection probability into the
estimates of density factor out the influence of grass on detection
probability?

James Tucker

you're modelling detectability.  In the other case, you're modelling how
density varies spatially.  In both cases, the covariates are treated as
constants.  No new issue arises if you use the same covariate in both
models.  There is an issue of propagation of error, because the
detectabilities are estimates, and you need some way to allow for this
when fitting the density surface, e.g. by bootstrapping the 2-stage
procedure.  But this is the case whether or not you have a covariate in
common between the models.

Steve Buckland
